purpose: Your bird touches the tip of a stick and follows it, which gives you a gentle way to guide your bird almost anywhere.
safety_notes: Keep sessions short.
Stop at the first sign of stress.
Never withhold food to make a bird hungrier for training.

name: Wing touch
purpose: Your bird is comfortable having its wings touched and gently opened, the way a vet does during an exam, and it stays relaxed the whole time.
safety_notes: Keep sessions short.
Stop at the first sign of stress.
Never withhold food to make a bird hungrier for training.
Keep touches brief, because long body contact can trigger hormonal behavior.
Never pull a wing that resists.
If your bird has an injury, arthritis, or a wing that doesn't open fully, ask your avian vet what's comfortable first.

name: Diet conversion
purpose: Your bird moves gradually from a seed-heavy diet to pellets, chop, and fresh foods while its weight stays steady.
safety_notes: Keep sessions short.
Stop at the first sign of stress.
Never withhold food to make a bird hungrier for training.
Watch droppings and appetite as well as weight. If your bird stops eating, put the usual food back and call your vet.
Some birds refuse new food so firmly that they stop eating. If your bird isn't eating, go back to the usual food today and call your vet.
Weigh in grams at the same time every day. A few grams matter on a bird.
Take uneaten fresh food out after a few hours so it doesn't spoil.
How much to feed varies from bird to bird, even within a species. Your vet can tell you what's right for yours.
safeguards: Daily weigh-ins are part of the whole journey, and the journey shows the weight trend right on its page.
The old food is never removed until the bird is reliably eating the new one.
If weight drops, the journey pauses with a clear message to call your avian vet.
The template suggests a vet check before starting, especially for older birds or birds on an all-seed diet.

name: Recall
purpose: Your bird comes to you when you call its name, whether that means flying across the room or walking along a perch. It's the most important safety skill if your bird ever gets out.
safety_notes: Keep sessions short.
Stop at the first sign of stress.
Never withhold food to make a bird hungrier for training.
